passages.original: Praelocutioni tamen optime diuinum subdidistis exemplum, quod ita quadratis constat alloquiis, ut ipsum in eo Chrysippum tenere lineam putes: peccatori dicit deus: quare tu enarras iustitias meas? huic dicto conserentes quasi ad sacerdotes apostropham: "quia beati Petri apostoli uicarius aestimatur, prohibetis archiatrum eius corpori adferre medicinam: quomodo uos animae eius curationem exhibere renuitis ?" magnum per diuina ridiculum an maxima lamenta sint nescio.
passages.english: To your preamble, however, you very aptly appended a divine example, which is made up of such well-squared phrases that you would think Chrysippus himself was holding the line in it: "To the sinner God says: Why do you recount my righteous deeds?" Joining to this saying an apostrophe, as it were, to the priests: "Since he is regarded as the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter, you forbid his chief physician to bring medicine to his body; how [is it that] you refuse to offer care for his soul?" Whether, by things divine, this is a great absurdity or matter for the greatest lamentation, I do not know.
passages.notes: The quotation is Psalm 49(50):16. "Quadratis ... alloquiis" (well-squared, i.e. neatly balanced phrases) and "tenere lineam" (to hold the line or rule) are ironic praise of the opponents' logical style, alluding to the Stoic logician Chrysippus. "Archiatrum" (chief physician) is apparently the court or papal physician. The quoted sentence is compressed in the Latin: the "his" of "his body" and "his soul" refers to the one regarded as Peter's vicar, i.e. the pope. "Per diuina" is taken as an oath ("by things divine"); it could instead mean "through divine [words]".
